title: A Fall Before Midnight

setting.name: Bellweather
setting.summary: A small English village: a square, a manor with its greenhouse and boathouse on the river, an inn, the church vestry, a doctor’s surgery, a post office, a railway halt and a disused mill. Someone is dead; the investigation begins the next morning.

story: The vicar found out that the postmistress had been steaming open the village's letters, and he told her he would report her. She waited for him on the garden steps at Vale Manor and pushed him down them, while two lovers lied about where they had spent the night.

rules.text: Bellweather's telephone exchange is the switchboard in the post office; at night the postmistress works the board herself.

people.name: Clara Vale
people.voice: Composed, dry and exact; she chooses words like a woman choosing gloves. Polite to the point of chill with strangers, warmer once she respects you.
people.public: Edmund’s younger sister. She has run Vale Manor’s household for years and guards its privacy.

people.name: Rowan Pike
people.voice: A plain-spoken countryman: short, blunt, practical, with a gardener’s patience and the odd dour joke.
people.public: The manor’s groundskeeper. He lives among his glasshouses and says little to anyone.

people.name: Dr Iris Marsh
people.voice: Clinical and direct, with brisk warmth underneath; says exactly what she observed and no more.
people.public: The village doctor. Methodical and direct; she is called whenever anyone in Bellweather is hurt or ill.

people.name: Arthur Bell
people.voice: A gruff country constable: terse, dry and matter-of-fact, with a soft spot he hides badly.
people.public: The village constable. He has secured the scene and asked you to investigate; he will hear an accusation when you can back it with evidence.

people.name: Edmund Vale
people.voice: Loud, confident and used to being obeyed; bluff good humour that turns cold when crossed.
people.public: Master of Vale Manor: a man of fixed habits, generous in public and hard in private.

people.name: The Reverend Thomas Hale
people.voice: Gentle and rambling, with a scholar’s digressions and a surprising steel when conscience is touched.
people.public: Vicar of St. Alden’s these twenty years. Gentle, absent-minded, and trusted with more secrets than anyone in the parish.

people.name: Dorothy Pruett
people.voice: Brisk, prim and precise, with relish for procedure and a keen, disapproving memory for other people’s business.
people.public: The postmistress. Every letter, parcel and telegram in Bellweather passes over her counter, and she forgets nothing.

people.name: Jonah Reed
people.voice: Slow, weathered and wry; a river man who speaks in the present tense and weighs every word like a stone.
people.public: Keeper of the manor’s boathouse and ferryman when the river is up. He knows the water and keeps his own counsel.

objects.name: a door key
objects.desc: A small brass key stamped 'St A. V.', worn bright with use.

objects.name: a pocket notebook
objects.desc: The vicar's pocket notebook, kept in his locked vestry desk.

objects.name: a muddy boot print
objects.desc: A narrow-heeled print in the soft border by the manor's terrace steps.

objects.name: a telephone
objects.desc: The manor's telephone, which connects through the village exchange.

objects.name: a sealed envelope
objects.desc: The vicar's letter of complaint to the Postmaster General.

objects.name: a coil of eel line
objects.desc: A tarred eel line wound on a stick, with a cork float notched 'R.P.'

objects.name: an upturned seed tray
objects.desc: A slatted wooden seed tray from the glasshouses, face down in the terrace border.

objects.name: a scrap of mended netting
objects.desc: A patched fragment of fishing net, the knots fresh and tarred, snagged on the same boards as a lost line.

objects.name: a pair of evening shoes
objects.desc: Miss Vale's small grey suede evening shoes, damp from scrubbing.

objects.name: a scrap of notepaper
objects.desc: A torn sheet from the hall telephone pad, written on in a heavy hand.

objects.name: a pair of rubber waders
objects.desc: Rowan's thigh-high rubber waders, hung on a peg in the potting shed.

question.text: Who killed The Reverend Thomas Hale?

attitudes.content: Hale has caught her steaming open letters and means to write to the Postmaster General by Friday.
For years she has secretly opened and read the village's letters. If that comes out she loses her post and her good name.
To catch Hale alone as he leaves the manor dinner, stop him, and take back his letter of complaint.
To say she never left the post office all evening.
To dine at the manor, settle the glebe dispute, and walk home by the garden path.
To make Hale give way over the glebe field.
To put a trunk call through to his London agent before bed.
She is in love with Jonah Reed.
That Edmund, or the village, will learn she meets the boatman at night.
To shield Clara's name at any cost to himself.
Clara was with him at the boathouse from just before ten until near eleven.
Once her visit is known, to clear Clara of the killing by vouching for her.
To spend the evening at the boathouse mending nets.
To set his eel lines by the boathouse after dark.
To start his morning rounds at the manor at first light.
To keep the peace and answer any call.
To attend whenever she is called.
To sort the morning mail bags.
That Edmund will dismiss him if he learns Rowan sets eel lines on the manor's water without leave.
To keep Miss Vale, who has always been kind to him, out of trouble and out of gossip.
To cover the small print by the steps and say nothing of the river, until his own presence there is proved.
To move his snagged eel line further under the boathouse boards before anyone finds it, tangling it with Jonah's mending scraps so it cannot be told apart without help.
That the river mud on her evening shoes will show she walked down to the boathouse last night.
Once Jonah has vouched for her, to hand over her shoes rather than let him be doubted.
That the village will learn he is quietly raising a mortgage on Vale Manor through his London agent.
To say nothing of his late trunk call to London unless it is plainly found out.
With the constable about to arrive, to burn the telephone note naming his London agent before anyone reads it.
If anyone asks why his waders are wet, to say he was clearing weed from the old mill race, far from the boathouse.

events.summary: Dorothy sorts mail at the post office, then slips out.
Dorothy waits in the dark beside the manor's terrace steps.
Edmund, Clara and the vicar dine at the manor; Edmund argues over the glebe field.
The vicar and Edmund talk in the study; neither gives way.
The vicar leaves by the garden door toward the terrace steps.
Dorothy confronts Hale on the terrace steps and pushes him; he falls to the stone below.
The vicar dies of a broken neck at the foot of the steps.
Dorothy takes the sealed complaint letter from Hale's coat and flees.
Dorothy gets back to the post office and takes her place at the board.
Edmund smokes alone in his study at the front of the house.
Edmund rings the exchange for a trunk call; nobody answers the board.
Edmund gives up on the call and goes to bed.
Clara meets Jonah in secret at the boathouse.
Clara creeps back into the manor and goes to bed.
Jonah mends nets at the boathouse.
Jonah stays at the boathouse for the night.
Rowan potters in his glasshouses.
Rowan sets eel lines on the bank beside the boathouse and watches them.
Rowan goes home to bed.
Constable Bell spends a quiet evening at his house on the square.
Dr Marsh writes up her notes at the surgery and retires.
On his morning rounds Rowan finds the vicar dead at the foot of the terrace steps.
Rowan rouses Edmund and Clara.
Rowan fetches Constable Bell from the square.
Rowan fetches Dr Marsh from her surgery.
Bell secures the steps and searches the body's pockets.
Dr Marsh examines the body: neck broken in a fall down the stone steps.
Packing up in the dark, Rowan loses one eel line, snagged fast in the reeds below the boathouse.
Seeing a small woman's print by the body, Rowan sets a seed tray over it before raising the alarm.
Before his rounds, Rowan wades out and pushes his snagged eel line deeper under the boathouse boards.
Clara scrubs river mud from her evening shoes at the scullery sink and hides them.
Edmund tears his note from the hall pad and burns it in the cold study grate; it only half burns.
Rowan hurries back from the river and hangs his dripping waders on the potting-shed peg before his rounds.

signs.speaker: clara
signs.title: Clara Vale on the evening
signs.text: We dined and sat rather late over Edmund's business with the glebe field, and once that was done I confess my head was aching dreadfully, so I went up and did not come down again until all the shouting this morning. I am afraid there is very little else to tell.
signs.ask: Where were you last night?
signs.surface_why: She claims she went up with a headache and stayed in her room all night, but she actually slipped out to secretly meet Jonah at the boathouse, then crept back in and had to scrub river mud off her shoes afterward - she was not in her room the whole time.
signs.show: Clara Vale says she dined late over Edmund's glebe field business, then went up with a headache and didn't come down until the shouting this morning. Do you know if that's true?
signs.confront: You told me you dined late over the glebe field business, then went up with a headache and stayed there until the shouting this morning. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: rowan
signs.title: Rowan Pike on the morning
signs.text: On my morning rounds, about half past six, I come upon the vicar lying dead at the foot of the terrace steps, and I raised the alarm sharpish. About twenty-five to seven I roused Edmund and Clara, then at quarter to seven I fetched Constable Bell from the square, and about ten to seven I fetched Dr Marsh from her surgery.
signs.ask: What did you do this morning?
signs.show: Rowan Pike says he found the vicar dead at the foot of the terrace steps on his morning round, and raised the alarm straight away. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me you found the vicar dead at the foot of the terrace steps about half past six, then roused the house and fetched help. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: edmund
signs.title: Edmund Vale on the morning
signs.text: Rowan roused Clara and myself at about twenty-five to seven. Until then I was abed, and I've nothing more to report of the morning.
signs.ask: What did you do this morning?
signs.show: Edmund Vale says Rowan roused him and Clara at about twenty-five to seven, and that he knows nothing of the morning before that. Does that match what you recall?
signs.confront: You told me Rowan roused you and Clara at about twenty-five to seven, and that you knew nothing more of the morning. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: clara
signs.title: Clara Vale on the morning
signs.text: At about twenty-five to seven, Rowan roused Edmund and myself. I can tell you nothing of the hours before that.
signs.ask: What did you do this morning?
signs.confront: You said Rowan roused you and Edmund at about twenty-five to seven, and that you knew nothing of the hours before. Is that so?
signs.show: Clara Vale says Rowan roused her and Edmund at about twenty-five to seven, but she knows nothing of the hours before. Does that match what you know?

signs.speaker: jonah
signs.title: Jonah Reed on the evening
signs.text: I spend the evening mending my nets, as a river man does, and turn in for the night when the lamp gives out. Nothing more in it than that.
signs.ask: Where were you last night?
signs.surface_why: He claims nothing happened beyond mending nets and turning in, but in truth he secretly met Clara Vale at the boathouse that evening—an omission that amounts to a false denial ('nothing more in it than that').
signs.show: Jonah Reed says he spent the evening mending his nets and turned in when his lamp gave out. Do you know if that's true?
signs.confront: You told me you spent the evening mending nets and went to bed when your lamp failed. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: dora
signs.title: Dorothy Pruett on the evening
signs.text: I was at the post office sorting the mail same as always, and I never left the board the whole evening.
signs.ask: Where were you last night?
signs.show: Dorothy Pruett says she was at the post office sorting mail all evening and never left the board. Can you confirm that?
signs.confront: You told me you were sorting mail at the post office and never left the board the whole evening. Is that so?

signs.speaker: edmund
signs.title: Edmund Vale on the evening
signs.text: We dined, and Hale and I had words in the study that settled nothing between us. After he left I sat up a good while smoking alone before I turned in for the night.
signs.ask: Where were you last night?
signs.surface_why: He leaves out the failed trunk call to the exchange, but everything he states—dinner, the argument, smoking alone, going to bed—is true; omission of a minor detail isn't a false claim.
signs.show: Edmund Vale says he dined and had words with the vicar in the study, then sat up smoking alone before turning in. Do you know if that's so?
signs.confront: You told me you dined, had words with the vicar in the study, then sat up smoking alone before bed. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: bell
signs.title: Arthur Bell on the evening
signs.text: Quiet evening at home on the square, as usual, and then to bed.
signs.ask: Where were you last night?
signs.show: Arthur Bell says he had a quiet evening at home on the square, as usual, before going to bed. Do you know anything that contradicts that?
signs.confront: You said you spent a quiet evening at home on the square, as usual, before going to bed. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Iris Marsh on the evening
signs.text: I was at the surgery writing up my notes, and then I retired for the night.
signs.ask: Where were you last night?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she was at the surgery writing up her notes before retiring for the night. Does that match what you recall?
signs.confront: You told me you were at the surgery writing up your notes before retiring for the night. Is that so?

signs.speaker: rowan
signs.title: Rowan Pike on the evening
signs.text: I was about my glasshouses most of the evening, same as always, then home and off to bed. Nothing much else to tell of it.
signs.ask: Where were you last night?
signs.surface_why: He omits the eel lines and the one lost in the reeds, but his vague account of glasshouse work and going home to bed doesn't contradict what actually happened.
signs.show: Rowan Pike says he spent most of the evening about his glasshouses before going home to bed. Do you know if that's true?
signs.confront: You told me you were about your glasshouses most of the evening, then home to bed. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: The doctor’s examination notes
signs.text: Examination of the deceased shows injuries from a fall. Death was from injuries from a fall, and it occurred between ten past ten and half past ten.
signs.show: The doctor's examination shows the vicar died of injuries from a fall, between ten past ten and half past ten that night. Does that square with what you saw?

reactions.bell: Aye, that's what the doctor found — neck broken from the fall down those steps, between ten past and half past ten. Matches what I saw when I went through his pockets myself.
reactions.dora: Ten past to half past, you say? Well, I was at the board sorting mail all evening, same as ever, so that's no business of mine.
reactions.iris: Yes, that's my finding exactly — a fall, neck broken, death between ten past and half past ten. I stand by my notes.

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Marsh on the body
signs.text: Death was from injuries from a fall, and it occurred between ten past ten and half past ten.
signs.ask: Doctor, what did you find when you examined Mr Hale?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says death came from injuries from a fall, occurring between ten past ten and half past ten. Do you agree with that finding?
signs.confront: You told me death was from injuries from a fall, between ten past ten and half past ten. Is that your settled conclusion?

signs.speaker: bell
signs.title: Arthur Bell on the morning
signs.text: Rowan fetched me from the square at quarter to seven, and I was present when Dr Marsh examined the body at five past seven and found the neck broken from a fall down the stone steps.
signs.ask: What did you do this morning?
signs.confront: You told me Rowan fetched you at quarter to seven, and that you were present when Dr Marsh found the neck broken from a fall down the stone steps. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Arthur Bell says Rowan fetched him from the square at quarter to seven, and he was there when Dr Marsh found the neck broken from a fall down the stone steps. Does that match what you know?

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Iris Marsh on the morning
signs.text: I was fetched by Rowan from my surgery at about ten to seven, and at five past seven I examined the body and found the neck broken from a fall down the stone steps.
signs.ask: What did you do this morning?
signs.confront: You told me Rowan fetched you at about ten to seven, and that at five past seven you examined the body and found the neck broken from a fall down the stone steps. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says Rowan fetched her from her surgery and that when she examined the body she found the neck broken from a fall down the stone steps. Does that square with what you saw?

signs.title: A print by the steps
signs.text: Under a slatted seed tray in the soft border by the top of the terrace steps there is one fresh print. It has a narrow heel and a short sole, a small woman's shoe, and the toe points down the steps. The gravel path holds no other clear mark.
signs.unlock: Once Rowan has admitted Miss Vale was at the boathouse all that time, he owns up that at dawn he put a seed tray over a print by the steps to protect her, and he lifts it.
signs.show: I found a single fresh print hidden under a seed tray by the top of the terrace steps, a small woman's shoe pointing down. Do you know whose shoe left that mark?

reactions.dora: A print, you say. Half the village walks that path, Inspector, and small shoes are hardly a rarity among the women hereabouts. I'm sure I couldn't tell you whose it is.

signs.title: Pike's eel lines
signs.text: "That's mine, right enough. Squire don't know I fish his water. Had my lines out by the boathouse. Miss Vale come down the path just shy of ten and went in. Didn't come out till near eleven. So she weren't up by them steps. Lost a line in the dark. Waded out at dawn and shoved it under the boards. Weren't the mill race."
signs.speaker: rowan
signs.ask: This line with your float on it was in the reeds by the boathouse, Mr Pike. Were you down there last night?
signs.unlock: Shown his own notched float from the reeds, Rowan can no longer deny he was by the boathouse last night, and he tells what he saw there.

reactions.dora: Pike's business with his lines is his own affair, not mine. I've told you plainly where I was all evening, and I don't see what his eel-fishing has to do with me.
reactions.clara: Pike is mistaken about the hour, I think, though I will not quarrel with a man over his eel lines. Very well — I did go down to the boathouse, but it was only to walk, and I came in and went straight to bed. I'd rather have told you myself than had it dragged out by a poacher's lantern.

signs.show: Rowan Pike admits the eel lines by the boathouse are his, fished without the squire's leave, and says he saw someone come down the path just before ten and not leave till near eleven. Do you know anything of that?
signs.confront: You've told me those eel lines by the boathouse are yours, fished without the squire's knowledge. Is that the whole of it?
signs.direct: Pike says he saw you go down to the boathouse just before ten and not come back up till near eleven, well clear of those steps. Is that so?

signs.title: Miss Vale's evening
signs.text: "Mr Hale dined with us. I went up at ten with a headache and did not come down again until Pike's shouting this morning. I am afraid that is all there is to tell."
signs.speaker: clara
signs.ask: Where were you last night, Miss Vale?
signs.show: Miss Vale says she went up with a headache at ten and didn't come down again till the shouting this morning. Does that square with what you saw?
signs.confront: You told me you went up with a headache at ten and stayed there till the shouting this morning. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: The boatman's night
signs.text: "I mend nets. The river is quiet, so I mend nets. Nobody comes down here of a night. Nobody came."
signs.speaker: jonah
signs.ask: Where were you last night, Mr Reed?
signs.surface_why: He claims nobody came to the boathouse that night, but Clara secretly met him there.
signs.show: Jonah Reed says he spent the night mending nets at the boathouse and that nobody came down there at all. Can you confirm that?
signs.confront: You told me you were mending nets all night and that nobody came down to the boathouse. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: The boatman gives way
signs.text: "Pike sees her, then. Well. She comes down a little before ten. She sits by my stove and we talk, that is all. She goes back up the path near eleven. She is never near those steps. You put that down plain."
signs.speaker: jonah
signs.unlock: Told that Rowan Pike saw Miss Vale go into the boathouse, Jonah stops denying the visit and vouches for her to keep her clear of the killing.
signs.ask: Mr Pike saw Miss Vale come to the boathouse last night. Was she with you?

reactions.clara: Yes. I told you a falsehood about the headache, Inspector, because I did not wish Edmund—or anyone—to know I go down to the boathouse. Mr Reed speaks the truth; I was with him, nothing more.
reactions.dora: That's Mr Reed's business and none of mine, and I'm sure I don't see what it has to do with the post office. I was at my board all evening, sorting the bags, same as always. I'll not be drawn into tittle-tattle about who sat where by whose stove.

signs.show: Jonah Reed now says a woman came down to the boathouse a little before ten, sat talking with him by the stove, and went back up near eleven, nowhere near the terrace steps. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You've now told me a woman sat with you by the stove from before ten till near eleven, and never went near those steps. Is that the whole of it?
signs.direct: Reed says you came down to his boathouse a little before ten, sat talking by his stove, and left near eleven, nowhere near those steps. Is that right?

signs.title: The squire's account
signs.text: "Hale dined here. We had words over the glebe field, words, mind you, nothing more. He went out by the garden door about five past ten. Said the path was quicker. I sat with a cigar in the study, then went to bed."
signs.speaker: edmund
signs.ask: Where were you last night, Mr Vale?
signs.confront: You told me the vicar left by the garden door past ten after your words over the glebe field, and you sat with a cigar before bed. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Edmund Vale says the vicar dined with him, they had words over the glebe field, and the vicar left by the garden door about five past ten while he sat alone with a cigar. Do you know if that's true?
signs.surface_why: He claims the vicar left by the garden door around 10:05 after dinner, but in truth the vicar and Edmund continued arguing in the study afterward; he also omits the phone call and burning the note, implying a simpler, false sequence of events.

signs.title: The postmistress's evening
signs.text: "I was at the post office the whole evening, sorting the morning bags, as I do every night. I keep proper hours. I do not go wandering about after dark."
signs.speaker: dora
signs.ask: Where were you last night, Miss Pruett?
signs.show: Miss Pruett says she was at the post office all evening sorting the morning bags and never went out after dark. Can you confirm she keeps those hours?
signs.confront: You told me you were sorting bags at the post office all evening and never went out after dark. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: An unanswered board
signs.text: "Private business, and I'll thank you to keep it so. Yes, I tried for a trunk call to London at half past ten. I rang the exchange a good five minutes and there wasn't a soul on the board. I gave it up and went to bed in a temper."
signs.speaker: edmund
signs.ask: This scrap from your grate, and these words pressed into your hall pad, Mr Vale. Did you try to put a call through last night?
signs.reading: The night board is in the post office and the postmistress works it herself. If nobody answered at half past ten, she was not at the board then, though she says she was there all evening.
signs.unlock: Shown the half-burnt scrap in his own hand and the words pressed into his hall pad, Edmund can no longer keep quiet about the call. He grudgingly says what happened when he rang the exchange.
signs.show: Mr Vale says he tried a trunk call to London at half past ten and got no answer from the exchange before giving up for bed. Does that tally with what you know?
signs.confront: You told me you tried a trunk call to London at half past ten and gave it up when no one answered. Is that the whole of it?
signs.surface_why: Matches the true events of the trunk call attempt and going to bed.

signs.title: A key in the waistcoat
signs.text: In the dead man's waistcoat pocket Constable Bell found a small brass key, worn bright, with 'St A. V.' stamped on the bow.
signs.show: Constable Bell found a small brass key stamped 'St A. V.' in the dead man's waistcoat pocket. Do you know what lock that key fits?

reactions.bell: Found that on him myself, right in the waistcoat pocket. Church key, by the look of the stamp—'St A. V.' Vicar'd have had cause to carry it, I'd think, nothing stranger than that.
reactions.edmund: A key? St A. V. — St Alden's Vicarage, I'd wager. No notion how it came to be on him, nor why it should concern me.
reactions.clara: St Alden's Vicarage, by the look of it. I couldn't say how he came to have it on him — that's hardly a household matter.

signs.title: The vicar's notebook
signs.text: Last entry, in the vicar's hand: 'Third complaint now. Letters to the Lodge come resealed, the gum still tacky. I have watched the counter myself. Told D.P. plainly on Tuesday: the steaming stops, or I write to the Postmaster General. Friday at latest. God forgive me, I take no pleasure in it.'
signs.unlock: The key stamped 'St A. V.' fits the locked desk in St. Alden's vestry; having also traced the eel line to Rowan's night by the water, there is reason to see what else that night turned up, and the notebook is inside the desk.

reactions.dora: That's a wicked thing to put in a dead man's book, and I'll not have my character blackened by it. The vicar had his fancies about the post, same as some folk have fancies about their neighbours, Inspector, and I never once laid a steaming kettle near another soul's letters.

signs.direct: I've read the vicar's notebook. He writes that letters to the Lodge come back resealed, and warns you plainly that the steaming must stop by Friday. Is that true?
signs.show: I've read the vicar's notebook, where he writes of letters to the Lodge coming back resealed and warns 'D.P.' that the steaming must stop by Friday. Do you know anything of that?

signs.title: A line in the reeds
signs.text: Freed from the knot of netting that half-buried it is a tarred eel line wound on a stick. The bait is still on the hook. A cork float is tied to it, with 'R.P.' notched into the cork.
signs.unlock: Once Jonah has told the netting from the line, the eel line itself can be drawn clear and its notched float read plain.
signs.direct: I found your eel line with its float notched 'R.P.' tangled in the netting, still baited. Can you tell me how it got there?
signs.show: In the netting at the boathouse I found a tarred eel line, baited still, with a cork float notched 'R.P.' Can you tell me whose line that is?

reactions.rowan: Aye, that's mine. R.P., same as I notch 'em all. Lost that one in the dark packing up, didn't fancy wading for it twice.

signs.title: A tangle under the boards
signs.text: Pushed well back under the boathouse landing is a knot of line and net together: a tarred eel line wound on a stick, and a patched scrap of netting snarled about it. The cork float is hidden from view, pressed against a crossbeam.
signs.unlock: The tarred twine and duckweed on Rowan's waders don't fit the old mill race, where nobody tars nets. The only tarred nets on the manor water are mended at the boathouse, so you wade the shallows under its landing.
signs.show: Pushed well back under the boathouse landing there's a knot of line and netting together, the float hidden against a crossbeam. Do you know how that got pushed in so deep?

reactions.rowan: That's my doing, Inspector, shoving it back under the boards with Jonah's netting so it wouldn't be found lying about loose. Didn't want the Squire hearing I fish his water, that's all there is to it.

signs.title: Mending the nets
signs.text: "That scrap's mine, right enough, from the net I patched that night. I know my own knots. If there's a line snarled in with it, it came after, pushed in deep where I'd not see it by lamplight."
signs.speaker: jonah
signs.ask: Mr Reed, do you know this scrap of netting found tangled with a line under your boards?
signs.unlock: Shown the tangle pulled from under the boards, Jonah recognises his own netting and can say the line was pushed in after his mending was done.
signs.show: Reed says the netting scrap is his own from that night's mending, but any line tangled with it must have been pushed in later, out of his sight. Does that match what happened?
signs.confront: You told me the netting scrap is yours from that night, but any line tangled with it was pushed in later, out of your sight. Is that the whole of it?
signs.surface_why: Matches the true events: Jonah did mend nets that night, and the line was indeed added later without his knowledge.

signs.title: Scrubbing at a Small Shoe
signs.text: You see Miss Vale with her sleeves pushed up, scrubbing a small grey suede shoe with a nail brush. When she sees you, she drops it away and dries her hands without saying anything.
signs.direct: I saw you at the scullery sink scrubbing a small grey suede shoe, which you dropped into the bucket when you noticed me. Can you tell me about that?
signs.confront: I saw you at the scullery sink scrubbing a grey suede shoe, and you dropped it into the bucket the moment you saw me. Why were you cleaning it in such a hurry?

reactions.clara: I'd rather not discuss my shoes, Inspector, if you don't mind. A lady may clean her own things in her own scullery without it being made a matter for the police.
reactions.edmund: Good lord, Clara, scrubbing shoes at this hour? I shan't ask — a man learns not to pry into his sister's housekeeping fancies.

signs.show: I saw Miss Vale at the scullery sink scrubbing a small grey suede shoe, which she dropped into the bucket and said nothing when she noticed me. Do you know anything about that shoe?

signs.title: The grey suede shoes
signs.text: A pair of small grey suede evening shoes, still damp. In the welts and under the instep there is fine grey silt with flecks of green duckweed and a broken bit of reed stem. There is no trace of the dark garden loam from the terrace border.
signs.unlock: Told that Jonah has vouched for her night at the boathouse, Miss Vale takes the shoes out from under the scullery sink and hands them over, so his word is not doubted on her account.
signs.direct: Your shoes here are damp with river silt and duckweed in the welts, and none of the terrace border's dark loam. Can you tell me where you were wearing them?
signs.show: These damp grey suede shoes have fine silt and duckweed in the welts, with no trace of the dark garden loam from the terrace border. Can you tell me where these were worn?

reactions.clara: Yes, those are mine. The silt is from the river path, not the terrace border—I was at the boathouse that night, as Mr Reed will tell you, and nowhere near where the vicar fell.
reactions.edmund: Pond silt and reed, is it? I'm sure Clara has her reasons, whatever they are — it's nothing to do with me or the house.
reactions.jonah: That's river silt and duckweed off my own bank, right enough. She came down to the boathouse that night, and I'll say plain she was with me there, nothing more owed to anyone for it.

signs.title: A scrap in the study grate
signs.text: In the study grate, among cold ashes from last night, lies a half-burnt piece of notepaper. Its top edge is ragged where it was torn from a pad. Above the charring, in a heavy hand: 'Trunk: Holborn 2271, Mr Gage, re Vale.' Everything below that has burnt to black flakes. A few spent matches lie on the hearth.
signs.unlock: Rowan saw the squire striking matches at an unlaid study grate, so you go and look through the ashes in it.
signs.direct: I found this half-burnt note in your grate naming a Holborn number, a Mr Gage, and the word 'Vale.' Can you tell me what that note concerned?
signs.show: In the study grate I found a half-burnt note reading 'Trunk: Holborn 2271, Mr Gage, re Vale,' with the rest burnt away and spent matches on the hearth. Do you know who wrote that note or what it concerned?

reactions.edmund: That's my hand, yes, and my business with my own agent, nothing to do with Hale's death. A man's entitled to burn his private correspondence without the whole county reading it over his shoulder.
reactions.clara: I know nothing of my brother's telephone calls or his ashes, I'm afraid — that's his study, and his business entirely, not mine to explain.

signs.title: The squire at the grate
signs.text: "When I'd roused 'em I went out through the hall for the constable. Squire was in his study, down on his knees at the grate, striking matches. There weren't no fire laid. Odd thing to be doing, with the parson lying out there."
signs.speaker: rowan
signs.ask: Mr Pike, what did the household do after you raised the alarm?
signs.show: Pike says that when he went for the constable, he saw the squire kneeling at the study grate striking matches, though no fire was laid. Can you tell me what Mr Vale was doing there?
signs.confront: You told me you saw the squire kneeling at the study grate striking matches with no fire laid. Can you tell me more of what you saw?
signs.surface_why: Accurately reports what he witnessed — Edmund kneeling at the grate striking matches — consistent with Edmund burning the note.

signs.title: The hall telephone pad
signs.text: The pad by the hall telephone has had its top sheet torn away roughly. When you tilt it to the window, the sheet below shows letters pressed deep into it: 'NO ANSWER. Try 8 a.m.' A cold cigar end, burnt right down, lies in the tray beside the instrument.
signs.unlock: The burnt scrap has the ragged top edge of a sheet torn off a pad. The only pad in the house is the one by the hall telephone, so you go and check it for the missing words.
signs.show: The telephone pad shows an impression reading 'NO ANSWER. Try 8 a.m.' with its top sheet torn away, and a burnt-down cigar end in the tray. Do you know who tore that sheet off and why?

reactions.edmund: Well. Yes. I tried the exchange at half past ten on a trunk call, London, my own business and none of the parish's. Nobody answered, I gave it up, burnt the note after - a man's entitled to burn his own scribblings, I should think.

signs.title: Waders on a peg
signs.text: On a peg in the potting shed hang a pair of rubber waders. They are wet to the thigh, and grey river silt is drying in the creases. A strand of black tarred twine is caught in one buckle, along with a few flecks of duckweed. A puddle has formed on the brick floor beneath them.
signs.direct: Your waders here are wet with river silt to the thigh, with tarred twine caught in the buckle and duckweed flecks. Can you tell me how they got that wet?
signs.show: In the potting shed I found a pair of waders wet to the thigh with river silt, tarred twine caught in a buckle, and duckweed flecks. Can you tell me whose waders these are and how they got so wet?

reactions.rowan: Them's mine, wet because I was down clearing weed from the old mill race, nothing more to it. Twine catches on everything down there, no mystery in that.

signs.title: Pike explains his waders
signs.text: "Wet? Course they're wet. Was out at first light clearing weed off the old mill race, same as every spring. Then up to the house on my rounds. That's all there is to it."
signs.speaker: rowan
signs.ask: Your waders are soaked through this morning, Mr Pike. Where were you wading?
signs.unlock: The waders are dripping on his own shed floor, so Rowan has to account for them when asked.
signs.show: Pike says his waders were wet from clearing weed off the old mill race at first light, same as every spring, before his rounds up at the house. Does that account match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me your waders were wet from clearing the mill race at first light before your rounds. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: edmund
signs.title: Edmund Vale saw Clara Vale
signs.text: I saw Miss Vale at Vale Manor at quarter to eight.
signs.ask: Did you see anyone last night?
signs.direct: Edmund Vale says he saw you at Vale Manor at quarter to eight. Is that so?
signs.show: Edmund Vale says he saw Clara Vale at Vale Manor at quarter to eight. Do you know if that's true?
signs.confront: You told me you saw Clara Vale at Vale Manor at quarter to eight. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: edmund
signs.title: Edmund Vale saw The Reverend Thomas Hale
signs.text: I saw Mr Hale at Vale Manor at quarter to eight.
signs.ask: Did you see anyone last night?
signs.direct: Edmund Vale says he saw you at Vale Manor at quarter to eight. Is that so?
signs.show: Edmund Vale says he saw Mr Hale at Vale Manor at quarter to eight. Do you know if that's true?
signs.confront: You told me you saw Mr Hale at Vale Manor at quarter to eight. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: When it happened
signs.text: The Reverend Thomas Hale died between 22:10 and 22:30.
signs.show: I understand the vicar died sometime between ten past ten and half past ten that night. Does that fit with what you know?

reactions.dora: That's the hour given, and I've nothing to add to it. I was at my board the whole evening, as I've said.

signs.title: Clara Vale's shoes
signs.text: Clara Vale wears small shoes.
signs.direct: I see you wear small shoes. Can you tell me about that?
signs.show: I've noticed Clara Vale wears small shoes. Had you noticed that yourself?

reactions.dora: I wouldn't know the size of Miss Vale's shoes, nor why it should concern me. I was at the post office all evening, as I've told you plainly enough.
reactions.clara: I do, yes, a small foot runs in the family. I don't see what my shoes have to do with anything, Inspector.
reactions.edmund: Small feet, yes, always has had, since she was a girl. I don't see what that's to do with Hale lying dead on my steps.

signs.title: Dorothy Pruett's shoes
signs.text: Dorothy Pruett wears small shoes.
signs.direct: I see you wear small shoes. Can you tell me about that?
signs.show: I've noticed Dorothy Pruett wears small shoes. Had you noticed that yourself?

reactions.dora: I have a small foot, as does half the village, I shouldn't wonder. I don't see what my shoes have to do with the vicar's death.

signs.title: Edmund Vale's shoes
signs.text: Edmund Vale wears large shoes.
signs.direct: I see you wear large shoes. Can you tell me about that?
signs.show: I've noticed Edmund Vale wears large shoes. Had you noticed that yourself?

reactions.dora: Large shoes, is it? Well, mine are small, as anyone in the village will tell you, and I never stirred from the post office board all evening, sorting the morning bags as I always do.
reactions.clara: That is quite true, my brother has always worn large boots, it has nothing to do with me, I'm sure. I went up with my headache and stayed there, as I've told you.
reactions.edmund: Yes, large shoes, always have been, and I don't see what my feet have to do with any of this. I sat up with my cigar and went to bed, as I've said.

signs.title: Jonah Reed's shoes
signs.text: Jonah Reed wears large shoes.
signs.direct: I see you wear large shoes. Can you tell me about that?
signs.show: I've noticed Jonah Reed wears large shoes. Had you noticed that yourself?

reactions.jonah: Large feet, aye, always have been. Runs in my family, nothing more to make of it.
reactions.dora: Big boots don't interest me, Constable. I was at the post office sorting bags, same as every night, and that's all I can tell you.

synopsis: The Reverend Thomas Hale was found dead at Vale Manor.

moods.iris: Alert and ready, bag in hand, waiting for whoever calls her next.
moods.bell: Steady and watchful, going about his duties and ready to answer any summons.
moods.edmund: Brisk and irritable, eager to be rid of certain papers before the constable arrives.
moods.dora: Quietly going about her morning post, a little subdued by the news.
moods.jonah: Guarded and resolved, ready to speak up the moment it might shield Clara.

clara: Edmund Vale is my elder brother, and I have kept his house since I came to live here.
I know Rowan as the groundskeeper, Dr Marsh as the village doctor, and Constable Bell as the man who keeps order in the square.
I live at the manor and keep my own things in my room there, as any lady of the house would.
rowan: I am groundskeeper at Vale Manor, and I live among the glasshouses, tending the gardens and grounds.
I know Mr and Miss Vale as my employers, and I know Jonah from working near the boathouse on manor land.
I know Constable Bell and Dr Marsh as the village's constable and doctor, called on when needed.
iris: I am the village doctor, and I attend to anyone in Bellweather who is hurt or ill, at my surgery or in their homes.
I know everyone in the village in the way a doctor does, from tending them or their families over the years.
I live and work out of my surgery, where I keep my medical bag and instruments.
I have no keys to the manor or elsewhere; I only attend when called.
bell: I am the village constable, keeping the peace and answering any call that comes.
I know everyone in Bellweather through my rounds and my duties in the square.
I live near the square, where villagers can find me if trouble arises.
I hold no personal keys to the manor or its outbuildings; that is not my place.
edmund: I am master of Vale Manor, and I keep to fixed habits in my days, overseeing the estate and its affairs.
Clara is my younger sister and keeps my household; Rowan is my groundskeeper and Jonah tends my boathouse.
I know Dr Marsh, Constable Bell, and Dorothy Pruett as the village's doctor, constable, and postmistress.
I live at the manor, where I keep my study and my papers.
I hold the keys to my own study and desk, as master of the house.
dora: I am the postmistress, and every letter, parcel, and telegram in Bellweather passes over my counter.
I know everyone in the village through my work at the post office, where I see them nearly every day.
I live and work at the post office, where I keep the mailbags and the till.
I hold the keys to the post office, as it is my charge to open and close it each day.
jonah: I am keeper of the manor's boathouse, and I ferry folk across the river when it runs high.
I know the Vale family as my employers, and I know Rowan from working the grounds near the water.
I live at the boathouse, where I keep my nets, oars, and gear.
I hold a key to the boathouse itself, as I am its keeper.

clara: I'm afraid I have nothing at all to offer you there.
That matter simply gives me nothing to tell you.
There is nothing further I can add on that score.
I have no answer to give you on that one.
rowan: Can't help you there, nothing to tell.
That's a blank for me, no more to say.
Nowt comes to mind, so I'll leave it there.
I've nothing on that, and that's the end of it.
iris: I have nothing to report on that particular point.
There's no observation I can offer you there.
I can't give you anything further on that matter.
That question yields nothing from me, I'm afraid.
bell: Nothing to tell on that one, I'm afraid.
Can't give you anything there, and that's that.
That's a blank page far as I'm concerned.
No more to say on that, closing it there.
edmund: I've nothing whatsoever to tell you on that.
That's simply not something I can speak to.
There's nothing more I can add there, man.
Nothing to give you on that score, I'm afraid.
dora: I have absolutely nothing to report on that matter.
That's a closed book as far as I'm concerned.
There's nothing further I can note down there.
No, nothing to add on that particular point.
jonah: Nothing there. River keeps that one, not me.
Can't give you a thing on that, no.
That one's empty for me, and stays empty.
Nowt to say there. That's the whole of it.
